chapter_text:
CHAPTER 1 — MEASUREMENT IN SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

Introduction

Measurement is the foundation of every science. Whether you want to know how tall you are, how hot today is, or how much sugar to add to a cup of tea, you are measuring. Science can describe a phenomenon in words; it can predict and verify it only after measuring it. This chapter introduces the precise language of measurement: physical quantities, units, the SI system, and the rules for combining and converting them.

1.1 NEED FOR MEASUREMENT

Measurement is a process of comparing a physical quantity with a chosen standard quantity. The standard quantity used in this comparison is called a UNIT. When we say a table is 1.5 metres long, we are saying that the length of the table is 1.5 times the standard 'metre'.

In ancient times people used informal standards: the length of a foot, the width of a palm, the span of a hand. These work for casual tasks but not for science or trade. Different people have differently-sized feet; the same person's foot grows over time. A useful unit must be agreed upon, reproducible, and unchanging.

1.2 PHYSICAL QUANTITIES AND UNITS

A physical quantity is anything that can be measured — length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, speed, energy, force, pressure, and so on. To express the value of a physical quantity we write:
    P = n u
where P is the value, u is the unit, and n is the numerical value (how many times the unit fits the quantity). The product n × u is the value; n and u are inseparable. '5' alone is not a length; '5 metres' is.

Properties a good unit should have:
  - well-defined and unambiguous,
  - of suitable size for the quantity being measured,
  - reproducible anywhere by anyone,
  - constant over time and place,
  - easy to use.

1.3 THE SI SYSTEM OF UNITS

The internationally accepted modern system of units in science is the Système International d'Unités, abbreviated SI. It rests on SEVEN base quantities, each with one defined base unit:

  Quantity                    Unit       Symbol
  Length                      metre      m
  Mass                        kilogram   kg
  Time                        second     s
  Electric current            ampere     A
  Thermodynamic temperature   kelvin     K
  Amount of substance         mole       mol
  Luminous intensity          candela    cd

Every other unit you will meet — newton, joule, pascal, watt, hertz, volt, ohm, and so on — is derived from these seven by combining them according to a formula. The newton, for instance, is 1 kg·m·s⁻².

1.4 DEFINITIONS OF THE SEVEN BASE UNITS

For reproducibility, each base unit has a precise scientific definition:

(i) Kilogram (kg): the mass of the international prototype of the kilogram (a platinum-iridium cylinder kept at Sèvres, France). Recent revisions of the SI redefine it through Planck's constant, but the operational value is unchanged.

(ii) Metre (m): the distance travelled by light in vacuum in a time interval of 1/299 792 458 of a second. This ties the metre to the universal constant c (speed of light).

(iii) Second (s): the time required for 9 192 631 770 vibrations of the radiation emitted by a transition between two hyperfine levels in the ground state of caesium-133.

(iv) Kelvin (K): 1/273.16 of the thermodynamic temperature of the triple point of water (the unique temperature and pressure at which ice, liquid water and water vapour coexist).

(v) Ampere (A): the current that, flowing through two long parallel wires of length one metre separated by one metre in free space, produces a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N between them.

(vi) Candela (cd): the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source emitting monochromatic light of frequency 540 × 10¹² Hz with a radiant intensity of 1/683 watt per steradian.

(vii) Mole (mol): the amount of substance containing as many elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, etc.) as there are atoms in 0.012 kilogram of carbon-12.

1.5 DERIVED UNITS

Units formed by combining the seven base units are called derived units. Examples:

  Area:         m² (square metre)
  Volume:       m³ (cubic metre)
  Speed:        m s⁻¹ (metre per second)
  Acceleration: m s⁻² (metre per second squared)
  Force:        kg m s⁻² (newton, N)
  Pressure:     kg m⁻¹ s⁻² (pascal, Pa = N/m²)
  Energy:       kg m² s⁻² (joule, J = N·m)
  Power:        kg m² s⁻³ (watt, W = J/s)
  Frequency:    s⁻¹ (hertz, Hz)
  Charge:       A·s (coulomb, C)

Several derived units have their own name and symbol; this makes equations easier to read.

1.6 SI PREFIXES

In the real world, quantities span many orders of magnitude — from the diameter of a hydrogen atom (~10⁻¹⁰ m) to the radius of the observable universe (~10²⁶ m). Writing all of these in plain SI units would be unwieldy, so SI provides standard prefixes:

  Multiple        Prefix    Symbol
  10²⁴            yotta     Y
  10²¹            zetta     Z
  10¹⁸            exa       E
  10¹⁵            peta      P
  10¹²            tera      T
  10⁹             giga      G
  10⁶             mega      M
  10³             kilo      k
  10²             hecto     h
  10¹             deca      da
  10⁻¹            deci      d
  10⁻²            centi     c
  10⁻³            milli     m
  10⁻⁶            micro     μ
  10⁻⁹            nano      n
  10⁻¹²           pico      p
  10⁻¹⁵           femto     f
  10⁻¹⁸           atto      a

Rules for using SI prefixes:
  - No space between prefix and unit symbol (kg, not k g).
  - A prefix is always used with a unit, never standalone.
  - Use only one prefix at a time (write 'pm', not 'mμm').
  - Prefixes are not used with the unit °C (write '25 °C', not 'k°C').
  - When raising a prefixed unit to a power, the power applies to the whole including the prefix: 1 cm² = (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m², not 10⁻² m².

1.7 RULES FOR REPRESENTING SI UNITS

(i) Leave a space between the numerical value and the unit symbol: '5 kg', not '5kg'. Exceptions: °, ′, ″ (no space) and °C (no space if SI usage convention).
(ii) Unit symbols are not pluralised. Write '5 kg', never '5 kgs'.
(iii) Unit symbols are not followed by a full stop unless they appear at the end of a sentence.
(iv) For compound units, leave a space between the base symbols: 'N m' (newton-metre) or use a dot 'N·m'. Slashes mean division: 'm/s'.
(v) Use the modifier with the unit name: 'newton metre squared' (not 'square metre newton').

1.8 SOME WORKED EXAMPLES

Example 1.  Convert 5 km to metres.
5 km = 5 × 10³ m = 5000 m.

Example 2.  Convert 3 hours to seconds.
3 h = 3 × 60 × 60 s = 10 800 s.

Example 3.  Convert a density of 8 g/cm³ to kg/m³.
8 g/cm³ = 8 × (10⁻³ kg) / (10⁻² m)³ = 8 × 10⁻³ / 10⁻⁶ kg/m³ = 8 × 10³ kg/m³ = 8000 kg/m³.

Example 4.  Express the speed of light c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s in km per hour.
3 × 10⁸ m/s × (1 km / 10³ m) × (3600 s / 1 h) = 3 × 10⁸ × 3.6 × 10⁻³ × 10³ km/h ≈ 1.08 × 10⁹ km/h.

SUMMARY

- Measurement compares a physical quantity with a standard (the unit). P = n × u.
- The SI system has 7 base units: metre, kilogram, second, kelvin, ampere, candela, mole.
- All other units in physics are DERIVED units formed by combining these seven.
- SI prefixes (k, M, G, m, μ, n, ...) scale base units up or down by powers of ten.
- A unit must be reproducible, of suitable size, well defined, and unchanging.
- Historic units like span, cubit and pace are not reproducible across people, hence the move to SI standards.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain why measurement is essential to science and daily life, and why informal body-based units (foot, palm, span) were replaced by standardised units.
State the relation P = nu connecting a physical quantity, its numerical value and its unit.
List the seven SI base quantities with their base units and symbols.
State the precise definitions of metre, kilogram, second, kelvin, ampere, candela and mole.
Express common derived units (newton, joule, pascal, watt, hertz, coulomb) in terms of the seven SI base units.
Recall the SI prefixes (kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro, nano, pico, etc.) and their numerical values.
Use SI prefixes and the rules for representing SI units to convert between units and write quantities correctly.
Classify given units as base or derived and justify the classification by tracing them back to the seven SI base units.

chapter_summary.title: Measurement in Science and Technology — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 1. It covers the role of measurement in science, the SI system of units (seven base units and a wide family of derived units), SI prefixes for scaling, and the precise rules for representing units in print.

sections.heading: Measurement and units
bullets: Measurement is a process of comparing a physical quantity with a standard quantity.
The standard quantity used to compare a physical quantity for its measurement is called a unit.
If a physical quantity P is 'n' times the standard quantity (unit) u, then P = n·u.
A good unit must be well-defined, of suitable size, reproducible everywhere, and unchanging in time and place.

sections.heading: The SI base units
bullets: The internationally accepted modern system of units in science is known as SI units (Système International d'Unités).
In SI there are 7 base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), kelvin (temperature), ampere (electric current), candela (luminous intensity), and mole (amount of substance).
Kilogram: the mass of a particular cylinder made of platinum-iridium alloy kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in France.
Metre: the distance travelled by light in vacuum in a time interval of 1/299 792 458 second.
Second: the time required for a caesium-133 atom to undergo 9 192 631 770 vibrations.
Kelvin, ampere, candela, and mole each have their own precise scientific definition.
The units obtained in terms of the base units are called DERIVED units.

sections.heading: Derived units
bullets: Common derived units: newton N = kg·m·s⁻² (force); joule J = N·m = kg·m²·s⁻² (energy); pascal Pa = N/m² (pressure); watt W = J/s (power); hertz Hz = s⁻¹ (frequency); coulomb C = A·s (charge).
Every derived unit can be written explicitly in terms of the seven base units.
Some derived units have a special name (newton, joule, ...) for readability; others are just compound symbols (m/s, m³).

sections.heading: SI prefixes
bullets: SI prefixes scale a unit up or down by powers of ten: kilo (k, 10³), mega (M, 10⁶), giga (G, 10⁹), tera (T, 10¹²); milli (m, 10⁻³), micro (μ, 10⁻⁶), nano (n, 10⁻⁹), pico (p, 10⁻¹²).
Prefixes let huge or tiny quantities be written compactly: 5 nm rather than 0.000 000 005 m; 2 GHz rather than 2 000 000 000 Hz.

Rules: no space between prefix and unit symbol; one prefix at a time; never used standalone; never with °C; when raising a prefixed unit to a power, the power applies to the whole prefixed unit (e.g. 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²).

sections.heading: Rules for representing SI units
bullets: Leave a space between the numerical value and the unit (e.g. 5 kg, not 5kg).
Unit symbols are NOT pluralised (5 kg, never 5 kgs).
No full stop after a unit symbol unless it ends a sentence.
For compound units, separate the symbols with a space or middle dot (N m or N·m).
When using powers with a unit name, the modifier goes after the name (metre squared, not square metre when the formal symbol is m²).

key_takeaways: Measurement compares a quantity with a standard: P = n × u.
SI has 7 base units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, candela, mole) — every other unit in physics derives from these.
Prefixes (k, M, m, μ, n, ...) scale units by powers of ten and make tiny / huge quantities readable.
A good unit is reproducible, of suitable size, well-defined, and unchanging — which is exactly why SI replaced informal body-based units.
SI notation has precise rules — leaving a space between value and unit, never pluralising symbols, never using two prefixes at once.

glossary.definition: The process of comparing a physical quantity with a chosen standard (the unit) and expressing the result as a numerical value times the unit.
A measurable property of a physical phenomenon or object, such as length, mass, time, temperature or electric current.
A standardised quantity used as a reference for measurement. The value of a quantity is expressed as a numerical multiple of the unit.
A unit belonging to the Système International d'Unités — the internationally agreed system that defines seven base units and many derived units.
One of the seven units fundamental to the SI system: metre, kilogram, second, kelvin, ampere, candela, mole.
A unit formed by combining base units according to a defining formula, e.g. newton = kg·m/s², pascal = N/m².
A standard prefix attached to a unit symbol to denote a power of ten — examples: kilo (10³), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶).
The unique temperature and pressure at which ice, liquid water and water vapour coexist in equilibrium — used in the definition of the kelvin.
The property of a unit by which any laboratory anywhere in the world can construct or measure it consistently. Essential for a scientific standard.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Measurement in Science and Technology (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-1 for Lesson 1. Attempt all questions. Most are open-ended and inquiry-based: observe your surroundings, measure, and explain in your own words.

questions.question: Measurement is an essential activity in our daily life. Observe your surroundings and ask yourself why this is important. Justify your answer with reasons.
questions.answer: Measurement is essential because every practical decision — cooking (how much rice, how much water), trade (a kilogram of fruit, a litre of milk), travel (distance, fuel), building (length of a beam), medicine (dose), even social activities (time of a meeting) — depends on agreed-upon quantities. Without measurement we could not compare, share, or reproduce results; communication between people and across cultures would break down. Science in particular cannot exist without measurement: a claim that 'water boils when hot enough' is meaningless until 'enough' is measured.
questions.explanation: Reasons should include comparison, sharing, reproducibility, and the role in trade / science / daily life.

questions.question: Measurement is a fundamental skill which is an essential part of our daily life activities. Choose any five objects from your surroundings with different materials and different dimensions. Make a table using suitable units (Name of object | Length/breadth/height | Weight | Area/Volume).
questions.answer:
Sample table (substitute your actual measurements):
  1. Medicine box: 15 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm; 50 g; volume 300 cm³.
  2. Notebook: 25 cm × 18 cm × 1 cm; 200 g; area 450 cm², volume 450 cm³.
  3. Cricket ball: diameter 7 cm; 160 g; volume ≈ 180 cm³.
  4. Steel water bottle: height 25 cm, diameter 7 cm; 350 g; volume ≈ 962 cm³ (πr²h).
  5. Ruler: 30 cm × 3 cm × 0.3 cm; 25 g; volume 27 cm³.
Report values with units; verify orders of magnitude make sense (a notebook should weigh hundreds of grams, not kilograms).
questions.explanation: Look for five sensible measurements with appropriate units (cm, m, g, kg, cm³, m³).

questions.question:
Make any two questions for the following passage:

'We express the result of measurement of a physical quantity by its value. The value of a physical quantity is made up of two parts, the numerical quantity and the unit, and it is equal to the product of both. Value of physical quantity = numerical value × unit.'
questions.answer:
Two possible questions:
  Q1. State the relation between the value of a physical quantity, its numerical value and the unit.
  Q2. If the mass of a stone is recorded as 4.5 kg, identify the numerical value and the unit. (Answer: numerical value = 4.5, unit = kg.)
Other sensible questions: 'Why can a numerical value never be quoted without a unit?'; 'If the unit changes, how does the numerical value change?' — etc.
questions.explanation: Two well-formed questions that probe the P = nu relationship, the role of the unit, or the consequences of changing units.

questions.question: Imagine that any unit can be used for any dimension. For example, can we measure distance in kilograms? (i) If yes, justify. (ii) If not, justify. (iii) Write the characteristics of a unit.
questions.answer:
(i) No — we cannot measure distance in kilograms.
(ii) The kilogram is a unit of MASS. It has the dimension of mass (M); a distance has the dimension of length (L). The two have different physical meanings: mass measures 'how much matter is in something'; length measures 'how far apart two points are'. A statement like '5 kg long' has no meaning. Units of different physical quantities are NOT interchangeable.
(iii) Characteristics of a good unit: (a) well-defined and unambiguous; (b) of suitable size for the quantity being measured; (c) reproducible by anyone, anywhere; (d) constant in time and place; (e) easy to use; (f) appropriate to the dimension of the quantity being measured.
questions.explanation: The key conceptual point is that a unit's dimension must match the quantity's dimension.

questions.question: The system of measuring devices has been there since ancient times. Various methods of measurement were adopted. Write the different methods of measurement used by our ancestors and explain how you found the above methods of measurement useful.
questions.answer:
Ancient measurements (Indian and global):
  Length: span (vitasti) — distance from thumb to little finger spread out; cubit (haath) — elbow to fingertip; foot (pad); pace; finger-width (anguli); dhanurmusti (bow-fist).
  Mass: ratti (red gunja seed); masha; tola; seer; maund.
  Volume: chhantak; ser; mun.
  Time: ghadi (~24 minutes); prahar (~3 hours).
Useful because: (a) always available — no tool needed; (b) easy to teach; (c) suitable for routine trade or building. Limitations: not reproducible across people (one person's span ≠ another's); changed with the person's growth; couldn't be standardised across regions for scientific work. Hence the eventual move to SI.
questions.explanation: Look for at least four ancient units (span, cubit, ratti, prahar, etc.) and a sensible 'useful but not standard' assessment.

questions.question: The exercise to redefine the system of units led to the birth of the current SI system. Comment on why the need was felt to redefine different systems of units defined and used by different countries.
questions.answer: Different countries historically developed their own systems (Imperial in UK/US, CGS in continental Europe, FPS, traditional Indian units). This caused: (i) trade friction — a kilogram in one country wasn't recognised in another; (ii) confusion in scientific publications — converting between systems is error-prone (the Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because of pound-vs-newton confusion); (iii) duplicated effort in instrument design and calibration; (iv) no clean way to do international science. Redefining a single, universally agreed system (SI) eliminates these problems: every laboratory measures the same metre, the same kilogram, the same second.
questions.explanation: Look for trade, science-communication, and reproducibility arguments.

questions.question: For measurement, each physical quantity has an SI unit assigned to it (e.g. 'metre for distance'). Units smaller and larger than the basic SI units can be converted using powers of 10 (e.g. 10⁻² m = 1 centimetre, 10³ m = 1 kilometre). Explain why we need different units for the same physical quantity.
questions.answer: Real-world quantities vary across many orders of magnitude. The diameter of an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m; the distance to a galaxy is about 10²² m. Expressing both in plain metres is awkward: '0.000 000 000 1 m' or '10 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 m' are hard to read, compare, and use in calculations. Prefixes (nm, μm, mm, cm, km, Mm, etc.) compress the number to something a human can read. The underlying physical quantity (length) is the same — only the unit prefix changes to match the scale of what's being measured.
questions.explanation: Answer should mention the wide range of physical scales and the convenience of compact representation.

questions.question: Take any book from your bag, measure its dimensions with a suitable scale, calculate the volume of the book. After measuring, convert the dimensions and volume into three different units used to measure that quantity.
questions.answer:
Sample (use your actual measurements):
  Book dimensions: length 25 cm, breadth 18 cm, thickness 2 cm. Volume = 25 × 18 × 2 = 900 cm³.

Convert to three different units of volume:
  (i) cubic centimetres (cm³): V = 900 cm³ (the measurement above).
  (ii) cubic metres (m³): 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. So 900 cm³ = 900 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 9.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
  (iii) litres: 1 litre = 1000 cm³. So 900 cm³ = 0.9 L.
  (iv) millilitres (bonus): 1 mL = 1 cm³, so 900 cm³ = 900 mL.

Similarly the dimensions:
  Length 25 cm = 0.25 m = 250 mm = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ km.
  Breadth 18 cm = 0.18 m = 180 mm.
  Thickness 2 cm = 0.02 m = 20 mm.

Verify the volume by multiplying the metre values: 0.25 × 0.18 × 0.02 = 9 × 10⁻⁴ m³ ✓.
questions.explanation: Look for a measured volume + three valid unit conversions using prefixes and dimensional reasoning.

questions.question: Presently we follow the SI system. The symbols of units obtained from names are indicated by special letters. Explain whether it is correct to write the units in the plural or to change the letter. For example, a unit of mass is gram, denoted by 'g' — can we write it as 'gm' or in plural as 'gs' or 'gms'? (i) If yes, justify. (ii) If not, justify. (iii) Explain how to follow the grammar of SI units.
questions.answer:
(i) No — these alternative spellings ('gm', 'gs', 'gms') are NOT correct in SI.

(ii) SI rules specify that unit symbols are fixed:
  - The symbol for gram is 'g' (not 'gm'). 'gm' is a colloquial abbreviation, not an SI symbol.
  - Symbols are NEVER pluralised. We write '5 kg', not '5 kgs'; '10 m', not '10 ms'.
  - Symbols are case-sensitive: 'g' (gram) is different from 'G' (giga, the prefix for 10⁹).

(iii) Grammar of SI units:
  - Space between numerical value and unit symbol: '5 kg', not '5kg'.
  - No full stop after a unit symbol (unless it ends a sentence).
  - Names of units (gram, metre) follow normal English plural rules in PROSE: 'five grams' is fine in a sentence. But the SYMBOL is never pluralised.
  - Symbols derived from a person's name are capitalised (newton N, joule J, hertz Hz); symbols not derived from a name are lowercase (gram g, metre m, second s).
  - One prefix at a time; no space between prefix and unit symbol (mg, not m g).
questions.explanation: Look for the key rule: unit SYMBOLS are fixed, case-sensitive, and never pluralised. Names in prose follow normal English plurals.

Classify the following: ms⁻², joule, kilogram, kelvin, watt, kilowatt-hour, second, metre. How many are BASE units?
questions.explanation: Base: kilogram, kelvin, second, metre. Derived: ms⁻², joule, watt, kilowatt-hour.

questions.question: Which of these units can be 'taken as a standard' for scientific work?
questions.explanation: Only the light-year (a defined multiple of c × second) is reproducible and standardised.

questions.question: Newton in terms of SI base units is
Joule in terms of SI base units is
Pascal in terms of SI base units is
A foot is a reliable scientific unit because everyone has feet.
questions.explanation: Foot size varies between people — not reproducible.

questions.question: The numerical value of a physical quantity is always the same regardless of unit.
questions.explanation: Changing the unit changes the numerical value: 1 m = 100 cm.

questions.question: The kelvin is one of the seven SI base units.
questions.explanation: Yes — temperature is a base quantity.

questions.question: The newton is an SI base unit.
questions.explanation: Newton is a derived unit (kg·m/s²); the base unit of mass is kilogram.

questions.question: The prefix 'k' (kilo) means 10³.
The prefix 'M' (mega) and 'm' (milli) mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: M = 10⁶, m = 10⁻³ — totally different. SI symbols are case-sensitive.

questions.question: It is correct to write '5kg' (no space).
questions.explanation: SI requires a space between the numerical value and the unit symbol: '5 kg'.

questions.question: It is correct to write '5 kgs' as the plural of kilogram.
questions.explanation: Unit SYMBOLS are never pluralised — 5 kg.

questions.question: Two prefixes can be combined, e.g. millimicrometre (mμm).
questions.explanation: Only ONE prefix at a time. Combine to a single prefix: nm.

questions.question: 1 cm² equals 10⁻² m².
questions.explanation: (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m². The power applies to the WHOLE prefixed unit.

questions.question: The value of a physical quantity P in terms of numerical value n and unit u is given by P = ____.
The SI base unit of length is ____.
The SI base unit of mass is ____.
The SI base unit of time is ____.
The SI base unit of temperature is ____.
The SI prefix giga represents ____ (as a power of 10).
The SI prefix nano represents ____ (as a power of 10).
The SI derived unit of force is the ____.
The SI derived unit of energy is the ____.
The SI derived unit of power is the ____.
The SI derived unit of pressure is the ____.
1 metre = ____ centimetres.
1 kilometre = ____ metres.
1 hour = ____ seconds.
The second is defined as the time required for a caesium-133 atom to undergo ____ vibrations.
questions.explanation: Defined value used in the SI definition of the second.

questions.question: Justify the statement: 'Measurement is an essential part of our day-to-day activities.'
questions.answer: From cooking (how much rice, how much water) to commerce (a kilogram of fruit, a litre of milk), travel (distance, time), and medicine (correct dose), every routine decision involves comparing a quantity against a standard. Without measurement we couldn't share recipes, sell goods reliably, schedule meetings, or build safe houses. In science it is even more fundamental — without measurement a 'hot' object and a 'cold' object cannot be distinguished objectively.

questions.question: In ancient times parts of the 'human body' were used for measurement. Give five examples.
questions.answer: Examples: span (vitasti) — tip of thumb to tip of little finger spread out; cubit (haath) — elbow to fingertip; pace — one walking step; foot — length of the foot; finger-width (anguli); palm-width (mushti); dhanurmusti (bow-fist).

questions.question: Why were ancient measurements replaced by SI units?
questions.answer: Ancient units like span, foot and pace were tied to a person's body and varied between individuals and even for the same individual over time. They could not be reproduced reliably between people, regions, or generations — making them unsuitable for science, international trade and engineering. SI units are precise, universally agreed, and reproducible anywhere in the world.

questions.question: Write three characteristics that a good unit should have.
questions.answer: (1) Well-defined and unambiguous. (2) Reproducible anywhere by anyone (does not depend on a specific person or place). (3) Constant in time — its size should not change. Additional desirable traits: suitable size for the quantity being measured, easy to use, dimensionally matched to the quantity.

questions.question: In the statement P = n × u, what do the symbols stand for?
questions.answer: P is the value of the physical quantity. n is the numerical value (a pure number — how many times the unit fits the quantity). u is the unit (the agreed standard). The value P is the product of n and u; n alone or u alone is meaningless.

questions.question: List the seven SI base quantities with their base units.
questions.answer: 1. Length — metre (m). 2. Mass — kilogram (kg). 3. Time — second (s). 4. Electric current — ampere (A). 5. Thermodynamic temperature — kelvin (K). 6. Amount of substance — mole (mol). 7. Luminous intensity — candela (cd).

questions.question: State the modern SI definition of the metre.
questions.answer: One metre is the distance travelled by light in vacuum in a time interval of 1/299 792 458 of a second. This ties the length unit to the universal constant c (speed of light).

questions.question: State the SI definition of the second.
questions.answer: One second is the time required for a caesium-133 atom to undergo 9 192 631 770 vibrations of the radiation corresponding to the transition between the two hyperfine levels of its ground state.

questions.question: Express the following in basic SI units: (i) newton, (ii) joule, (iii) pascal.
questions.answer: (i) Newton = kg·m·s⁻² (force = mass × acceleration). (ii) Joule = N·m = kg·m²·s⁻² (energy = force × distance). (iii) Pascal = N/m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻² (pressure = force / area).

questions.question: Classify as base or derived: newton, kilogram, m·s⁻², joule, kelvin, watt, kilowatt-hour, second, metre.
questions.answer: BASE units: kilogram, kelvin, second, metre. DERIVED units: newton (kg·m/s²), m·s⁻² (acceleration), joule (kg·m²/s²), watt (J/s), kilowatt-hour (kW × h, a unit of energy).

questions.question: Write the numerical values of the following SI prefixes: yotta, mega, micro, femto, yocto.
Represent the following measurements using a suitable SI prefix: (i) 2 × 10⁻⁸ s, (ii) 1.54 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, (iii) 1.98 × 10⁻⁶ mol.
Convert each into proper SI base units: (i) 1 litre, (ii) 10000 cm², (iii) 100 decigram, (iv) 760 cm of Hg column (height only).
What units are commonly used for: (i) potatoes, (ii) milk, (iii) silk ribbon, (iv) land area?
questions.answer: (i) Potatoes — kilogram (kg). (ii) Milk — litre (L) or millilitre (mL). (iii) Silk ribbon — metre (m) or centimetre (cm). (iv) Land area — square metre (m²) or hectare (1 ha = 10 000 m²); in India also 'acre' or 'gunta' locally.

questions.question: Give one example of (i) a physical quantity with neither unit nor dimension; (ii) one with unit but no dimension.
questions.answer: (i) Refractive index — pure ratio of speeds, no unit, no dimension. Also: strain, relative density. (ii) Plane angle (radian) and solid angle (steradian) — they have a NAMED unit but no fundamental dimension (ratios of lengths).

questions.question: Convert the following to SI base units: (i) metric tonne, (ii) light-year, (iii) year.
questions.answer: (i) 1 metric tonne = 1000 kg = 10³ kg. (ii) 1 light-year = distance light travels in 1 year ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s × 3.15 × 10⁷ s ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. (iii) 1 year = 365 × 24 × 3600 s ≈ 3.15 × 10⁷ s.

questions.question: Can a weighing machine with each division at 5 kg be used to weigh 2 kg of mango? Justify.
questions.answer: No, not accurately. The smallest division (least count) of the machine is 5 kg, meaning it can only distinguish between weights at 5-kg intervals (0, 5, 10, 15, ...). A 2 kg mass would round to either 0 or 5 — a huge relative error (40-50%). For 2 kg you need a scale whose least count is much smaller, say 10 g or 100 g.

questions.question: Cite one example showing that the power of a unit with a prefix is raised to the WHOLE prefixed unit, including the prefix.
questions.answer: Consider 1 cm². 'c' is the prefix centi = 10⁻². So 1 cm = 10⁻² m. Then 1 cm² = (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m². If the power applied only to the metre and not to the prefix, we would wrongly get 10⁻² m². Similarly 1 km³ = (10³ m)³ = 10⁹ m³, not 10³ m³.

questions.question: For measurement of which quantities are these traditional units used: (i) Gaz, (ii) Prahar, (iii) Quintal, (iv) kVAh?
questions.answer: (i) Gaz — length (about 0.91 m, like a yard). (ii) Prahar — time (about 3 hours; 8 prahars make a day). (iii) Quintal — mass (1 quintal = 100 kg). (iv) kVAh (kilovolt-ampere-hour) — apparent electrical energy in power-system billing.

questions.question: Why does the value of a physical quantity always have a unit?
questions.answer: A bare numerical value has no physical meaning. '5' could be 5 metres, 5 kilograms, 5 seconds, or 5 cars — completely different quantities. The unit fixes the dimension and meaning. Two values of the same physical quantity become comparable only when expressed in the same unit. Hence the universal rule: a measurement = numerical value × unit.

questions.question: State three rules for representing SI units in print.
questions.answer: (1) Leave a space between the numerical value and the unit symbol: '5 kg', not '5kg'. (2) Unit symbols are never pluralised — write '5 kg', not '5 kgs'. (3) No full stop after a unit symbol unless it ends a sentence. Additional rule: SI unit symbols are case-sensitive (g for gram vs G for giga).

questions.question: How will you measure the density of a solid block?
questions.answer: Density = mass / volume. (i) Measure the mass of the block on a balance. (ii) Measure the volume: for a regular block, use a ruler to measure length × breadth × height = volume; for an irregular shape, use the displacement method (submerge in a known volume of water and measure the rise). (iii) Compute density = mass / volume in kg/m³ or g/cm³.

questions.question: State the SI definitions of metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and ampere.
questions.answer:
Metre: the distance travelled by light in vacuum in a time interval of 1/299 792 458 second.

Kilogram: historically the mass of a particular cylinder of platinum-iridium alloy kept at the BIPM near Sèvres, France. Modern SI defines it via Planck's constant h.

Second: the time required for a caesium-133 atom to undergo 9 192 631 770 vibrations of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two hyperfine levels of its ground state.

Kelvin: 1/273.16 of the thermodynamic temperature of the triple point of water (the unique conditions at which ice, liquid water and water vapour coexist).

Ampere: the current that, when flowing through two long parallel wires of length one metre, separated by one metre in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ newton per metre of length between them.

questions.question: Tabulate the SI prefixes from yotta (10²⁴) down to yocto (10⁻²⁴), giving the prefix, the symbol, and the power of 10.
questions.answer: yotta Y 10²⁴; zetta Z 10²¹; exa E 10¹⁸; peta P 10¹⁵; tera T 10¹²; giga G 10⁹; mega M 10⁶; kilo k 10³; hecto h 10²; deca da 10¹; deci d 10⁻¹; centi c 10⁻²; milli m 10⁻³; micro μ 10⁻⁶; nano n 10⁻⁹; pico p 10⁻¹²; femto f 10⁻¹⁵; atto a 10⁻¹⁸; zepto z 10⁻²¹; yocto y 10⁻²⁴.

questions.question: Derive the SI base-unit expression for: (a) joule, (b) watt, (c) pascal, (d) newton.
questions.answer:
(a) Joule (energy) = force × distance = (kg·m/s²) × m = kg·m²·s⁻².
(b) Watt (power) = energy / time = (kg·m²·s⁻²) / s = kg·m²·s⁻³.
(c) Pascal (pressure) = force / area = (kg·m·s⁻²) / m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻².
(d) Newton (force) = mass × acceleration = kg × m·s⁻² = kg·m·s⁻².

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student measures the length of a table with two different rulers: one calibrated in centimetres, the other in inches. She records 120 cm and 47.24 inches.

(i) Is the physical quantity being measured the same in both cases?
(ii) Explain why the numerical values are different.
(iii) Verify using 1 inch = 2.54 cm.
(iv) Which expression is the 'true value' of the length?
questions.answer:
(i) Yes — both readings measure the same physical quantity (the length of the table). The thing being measured is unchanged.
(ii) The unit is different (cm vs inch), so by P = n × u, when u changes the numerical value n must change to keep P the same.
(iii) 47.24 inch × 2.54 cm/inch ≈ 120.0 cm ✓.
(iv) Both expressions are valid representations of the same length — neither is more 'true' than the other. SI conventions prefer the metric form (1.20 m or 120 cm).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The SI system has 7 base units. Every derived unit can be expressed in terms of these.

(i) List the 7 base quantities and their SI base units.
(ii) Express the joule in terms of SI base units.
(iii) Express the watt in terms of SI base units.
(iv) Why is the SI system preferred internationally over older systems like the FPS?
questions.answer:
(i) Length – metre (m); Mass – kilogram (kg); Time – second (s); Electric current – ampere (A); Thermodynamic temperature – kelvin (K); Amount of substance – mole (mol); Luminous intensity – candela (cd).
(ii) Joule = N·m = kg·m²·s⁻².
(iii) Watt = J/s = kg·m²·s⁻³.
(iv) SI is decimally based (powers of 10 via prefixes), uses precisely-defined reproducible standards, is internationally agreed and adopted by every major scientific community, and is internally consistent (all derived units flow from the seven base units).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A biologist describes a bacterial cell as 1 µm wide and a virus as 100 nm wide.

(i) Convert both widths into metres in scientific notation.
(ii) How many viruses fit across the width of one bacterium?
(iii) State the rule of exponents used.
(iv) If a cell is 10 µm wide, how many bacteria fit across it?
questions.answer:
(i) Bacterium: 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m. Virus: 100 nm = 100 × 10⁻⁹ m = 10⁻⁷ m.
(ii) Bacterium / virus = 10⁻⁶ / 10⁻⁷ = 10¹ = 10. Ten viruses fit.
(iii) Quotient rule of exponents: 10ᵃ / 10ᵇ = 10ᵃ⁻ᵇ.
(iv) 10 µm / 1 µm = 10. Ten bacteria fit across a 10-µm cell.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A shopkeeper sells fabric. A customer buys 2.5 m of cloth at ₹120 per metre. Another buys 175 cm of cloth at the same rate.

(i) Convert 175 cm to metres.
(ii) Compute the cost for each customer.
(iii) Whose purchase has the larger length?
(iv) State the conversion factor between metres and centimetres.
questions.answer:
(i) 175 cm = 1.75 m.
(ii) Customer 1: 2.5 × 120 = ₹300. Customer 2: 1.75 × 120 = ₹210.
(iii) Customer 1 has the larger length (2.5 m vs 1.75 m).
(iv) 1 m = 100 cm; equivalently 1 cm = 0.01 m.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A water tank measures 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m.

(i) Find its volume in m³.
(ii) Convert this volume into litres (1 m³ = 1000 L).
(iii) Convert into cm³.
(iv) If water flows in at 50 litres per minute, how long to fill the tank?
questions.answer:
(i) V = 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 m³.
(ii) 3 m³ × 1000 = 3000 L.
(iii) 3 m³ × 10⁶ cm³/m³ = 3 × 10⁶ cm³ = 3 000 000 cm³.
(iv) Time = 3000 L / 50 L per min = 60 minutes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Density is mass per unit volume.

(i) Write the SI unit of density.
(ii) The density of water is 1000 kg/m³. Convert to g/cm³.
(iii) An iron block has mass 7800 kg and density 7800 kg/m³. What is its volume?
(iv) Compare the density of iron with water — what does it tell you?
questions.answer:
(i) kg/m³ (kilogram per cubic metre).
(ii) 1000 kg/m³ × (1000 g / kg) × (1 m³ / 10⁶ cm³) = 1000 × 1000 / 10⁶ = 1 g/cm³.
(iii) Volume = mass / density = 7800 / 7800 = 1 m³.
(iv) Iron (7800 kg/m³) is 7.8 times denser than water (1000 kg/m³). That is why iron sinks in water and an iron block of the same volume as a water-filled bottle is much heavier.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Until 2019 the kilogram was defined using a physical artefact — the International Prototype of the Kilogram (IPK), a platinum-iridium cylinder kept in France. Today it is defined via a fundamental constant.

(i) Where was the IPK kept?
(ii) What problem with the IPK led to its redefinition?
(iii) Which fundamental constant is used in the modern SI definition of the kilogram?
(iv) Why is a definition based on a fundamental constant preferable to one based on an artefact?
questions.answer:
(i) At the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM) at Sèvres, near Paris, France.
(ii) The IPK's mass was found to drift very slightly over decades compared to its official copies. An artefact can be scratched, contaminated or eroded, so the standard itself was changing.
(iii) Planck's constant h.
(iv) A definition based on a fundamental constant of nature is reproducible in any well-equipped laboratory anywhere in the universe, doesn't depend on a single physical object that could be damaged or lost, and is invariant over time. Constants like c (speed of light) and h (Planck's constant) are universal — every observer measures them as the same value.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student is asked to compute the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s, using KE = ½ m v².

(i) Substitute the values and compute the numerical answer.
(ii) Express the unit of KE using base units, step by step.
(iii) What name and symbol does this unit have?
(iv) If the speed doubles, by what factor does KE change?
questions.answer:
(i) KE = ½ × 2 × 5² = ½ × 2 × 25 = 25.
(ii) Unit of m v² = kg × (m/s)² = kg × m²/s² = kg·m²·s⁻².
(iii) The unit kg·m²·s⁻² is the joule (J).
(iv) KE ∝ v². Doubling v multiplies KE by 4. So the new KE = 4 × 25 = 100 J.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A mobile-phone charger is rated 5 V × 2 A.

(i) Compute the power in watts.
(ii) Express the unit of power in terms of SI base units.
(iii) Energy used during 30 minutes of charging?
(iv) Express this energy in kWh.

Read the passage and answer the questions.

A classmate insists that '5 cm² equals 5 × (0.01) m² = 0.05 m²'.

(i) Test their calculation.
(ii) What rule have they violated?
(iii) State the correct calculation.
(iv) Convert 1 m² to cm² to double-check the relationship.
questions.answer:
(i) Their value is wrong. 0.05 m² is much too large.
(ii) They applied the prefix only to the centimetre, not to the WHOLE prefixed unit. The power-2 should apply to centi as well.
(iii) 1 cm = 10⁻² m, so 1 cm² = (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m². Therefore 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 0.0005 m² (not 0.05 m²).
(iv) 1 m² = 1 m × 1 m = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm². Confirms 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m².

questions.question: The SI prefix for 10²⁴ is
The SI prefix for 10⁻²⁴ is
How many micrometres are in 1 millimetre?
Convert 3.6 km/h to m/s.
A unit of mass can be used to measure length as long as the numerical value is large enough.
questions.explanation: A unit's dimension must match the quantity. Mass and length have different dimensions.

questions.question: The kelvin scale starts from absolute zero (the coldest possible temperature).
questions.explanation: 0 K corresponds to −273.15 °C — the theoretical minimum temperature.

questions.question: The SI base unit of luminous intensity is ____.
The SI base unit of amount of substance is ____.
Convert 36 km/h to m/s.
questions.answer: 36 km/h = 36 × (1000 m / 3600 s) = 36000/3600 = 10 m/s. Memorise: divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s.

questions.question: Convert 5 g/cm³ to kg/m³ step by step.
questions.answer: Start: 5 g/cm³. Convert grams to kg: multiply by 10⁻³. Convert cm³ to m³: divide by 10⁻⁶ (i.e. multiply by 10⁶). Combined factor = 10⁻³ × 10⁶ = 10³. So 5 g/cm³ = 5 × 10³ kg/m³ = 5000 kg/m³.

questions.question: Express the units of the following physical quantities in SI base units: (i) velocity, (ii) acceleration, (iii) momentum.
questions.answer: (i) Velocity = distance / time → m / s = m·s⁻¹. (ii) Acceleration = velocity / time → (m/s) / s = m·s⁻². (iii) Momentum = mass × velocity → kg × m/s = kg·m·s⁻¹.

questions.question: Show that 1 kWh equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joule. Hence find how many joules are in 5 kWh.
Why did the international scientific community move from a body-based unit system to the SI system? Give three specific reasons.
questions.answer:
(1) Reproducibility — body-based units (foot, span, cubit) vary between individuals and over time; SI units rest on universal constants (speed of light, atomic vibrations of caesium-133) that are the same for everyone.

(2) International commerce and science — different countries used different traditional systems. Trade and scientific collaboration require a single agreed standard. The SI provides that.

(3) Consistency and computation — SI is decimal (powers of 10 via prefixes), so unit conversions are easy. Derived units flow cleanly from the seven base units. Older systems (Imperial, FPS) had awkward conversion factors (12 inches in a foot, 16 ounces in a pound) that bred errors.
